title: introduce-queue-shaper-proportional-pacing-to-reduce-starvation-in-continuous-batching
author: Maya R. Chen
ci_checks: benchmarks/e2e: pass (two reruns due to noise)
description:
Motivation: Under mixed workloads with heterogeneous sequence lengths and KV-cache pressure, continuous-batching can produce starvation at the queue tail: long-lived short requests wait behind back-to-back large batches, and requests pinned to KV-heavy paths see increased tail latency. This PR introduces a lightweight queue-shaper with proportional pacing that biases batching windows to restore service-rate fairness without sacrificing packing efficiency.

What this change does: Implements a queue shaper and proportional pacing policy inside the continuous-batcher. The shaper tracks per-queue recent service bytes and served-request-count (exponentially weighted), computes a target paced-window for each queue, and adjusts batch admission windows to favor queues that have been under-served. The policy is kernel-aware in two ways: 1) it estimates effective per-token kernel time (hot vs quantized kernels) and folds that into the pacing budget; 2) it favors co-location with cached KV entries by adding a small priority boost for requests that hit the KV prefix cache.

Design notes (single-string section): The algorithm is intentionally conservative: a small smoothing factor (alpha=0.12) and a capped pacing multiplier (max 2.0) ensure we don't oscillate under transient spikes. Admission is still allowed if a request would otherwise breach latency SLOs (deadline-fallback), but the shaper reduces likelihood of repeated preemption for short requests. The implementation is fully local to the scheduler process and requires no cross-node coordination.

Files touched and high-level changes: Adds runtime/scheduler/queue_shaper.h/cpp, a pacing helper runtime/scheduler/proportional_pacer.cc, small hooks in runtime/scheduler/batcher.cc to query the pacer, a KV-prefetch hint in runtime/scheduler/kv_policy.cc, unit/integration tests under runtime/tests/queue_shaper_integration_test.py, and a micro-benchmark under benchmarks/continuous_batching/shaper_microbenchmark.py. Also adds a short design doc docs/design/queue-shaper.md and a feature flag toggle in deploy/feature_flags.yaml.

Performance summary: Microbenchmarks and cluster canary show: median P50 latency improves by ~8% for mixed short/long mixes (50:50), P95 tail for short requests reduced by 25-35% in KV-light scenarios, and P99 tail improved 18-30% under KV-heavy patterns. Overall throughput is within 1-3% of baseline; cost per token does not increase materially. Benchmarks include correctness sweep across quantized and full-precision kernels.

Testing and rollout: Unit + functional tests added. Benchmarked on perf-canary cluster over 48 hours with three workload mixes (algo-trading-like low-latency, chat-like mixed, and bulk-embedding). Gradual rollout plan: start behind feature flag in Dedicated pools (10% of capacity), monitor latency/throughput/traces and KV-hit telemetry, then expand to 50% and finally flip default after two weeks of stable metrics.

Risks and mitigations: Oscillation under pathological synchronized arrivals is mitigated with smoothing and a conservative cap. If pacing wrongly favors a queue, deadline-fallback preserves SLOs. Observability hooks added to Redwood Console (new metrics: scheduler.pacer.available_budget, scheduler.pacer.window_adjustments, scheduler.pacer.queue_deficit) to detect misbehavior.

Related: This complements previous queueing improvements (ticketed leases / deadline coalescing) by operating orthogonally at the pacing/admission layer. Linked Linear items ENG-4127 (scheduler fairness experiment) and ENG-4171 (KV-aware scheduling baseline) capture the experimentation history.

Checklist: code compiles and passes CI; unit and integration tests added; docs/design updated; rollout plan and feature flag included.

References: internal bench run IDs: perf/2026-02-24-shaper-A, perf/2026-02-25-shaper-B.

review_discussion: Liam O'Connor (reviewer): Can we quantify the cost of additional bookkeeping? Any thread-local contention?
Maya R. Chen (author): Bookkeeping is bounded and mostly atomic counters + EWMA per-queue. We measured <2% CPU overhead in the canary; no global locks added. Details included in design doc.
Priya Nair (reviewer): How does this interact with the existing ticket lease scheme? Could there be double-throttling?

Maya R. Chen (author): The shaper operates before ticket allocation and only adjusts admission windows. Ticket leases still enforce long-term fairness; we tested combined behavior in integration tests (see tests/shaper_vs_lease.py scenario).
Diego Ruiz (reviewer): Any regression on long-running throughput-heavy batched flows?
Maya R. Chen (author): Throughput stayed within 3% of baseline in our perf runs; large-batch paths are accounted for via kernel-time estimation so they aren't starved.
Sara Kim (approver): I'm fine with the conservative defaults. Approving for squash merge once CI is green.
release_notes: Introduce a queue shaper with proportional pacing to reduce starvation and tail latency in continuous-batching. Behind feature flag; default off for now. Improvements: reduced P95/P99 tail for short requests under mixed workloads. See docs/design/queue-shaper.md for details.
